text: On the morning of the twenty second of January, the United States military began preparing to photograph Columbia in orbit. Ninety minutes later it stopped.
Wayne Hale phoned a defence department representative at the Cape and asked the military to start the process.

text: The chair of the mission management team, Linda Ham, asked who was requesting the imagery. She called several senior managers. Each said they had not requested it, and could not identify a requirement for it.

text: The board's finding is narrow and it is precise. Ham has publicly said she did not know the debris assessment team wanted the images. The board does not dispute that. What it says is this.

text: She never asked them directly if the request was theirs, even though they were the team analysing the foam strike.

text: There is one more finding here, and it is the one almost nobody quotes.

text: Nobody in the chain of command had the security clearance to know what American imaging satellites could actually do. Not at NASA, not at the contractors. Nobody asked what quality of picture was even possible.
source: CAIB Report, Vol. I, ch. 6, p. 154

text: So the decision not to look was made by people who did not know what looking would have shown them. The board's phrase is that they were making critical decisions about imagery capabilities based on little or no knowledge.
